questions.stem: Larkspur's Orders table is too large to reload every night, and only about 1% of its rows change each day. Which load design fits best?

options.text: Load only rows whose OrderID is greater than the largest OrderID already loaded
Reload the whole table every night and overwrite the bronze copy
Load only rows whose LastModified is later than the high watermark saved by the last successful run
Take a weekly full copy and skip the days in between

questions.explanation: LastModified changes on every insert and update, so a watermark on it picks up new and changed rows while reading about 1% of the table. An OrderID watermark finds new orders but misses updates to old ones, a nightly full reload rereads 400 million rows to catch 4 million changes, and a weekly copy leaves data up to a week stale.

questions.stem: You are building a watermark-based incremental load from a SQL table into a lakehouse. Which three things does the design need? Each correct answer is part of the solution.

options.text: A stored watermark value from the last successful run
A full overwrite of the destination table on every run
V-Order turned off on the destination table
A source column whose value increases whenever a row is inserted or changed
A filter on the source query that reads only rows past the stored watermark

questions.explanation: An incremental load needs a column that moves forward when rows change, a place to keep the last value loaded, and a source query that reads only rows after it. The watermark is updated only after the copy succeeds, so a failed run is simply repeated. V-Order is unrelated, and a full overwrite is the opposite of an incremental load.

questions.stem: Put the activities of a watermark-based incremental copy pipeline in the order they run.

options.text: Save the new value as the stored watermark
Look up the stored watermark from the last successful run
Look up the current highest change value in the source table
Copy the source rows that changed between the two values

questions.explanation: The pipeline reads the old watermark and the new high value first, so the copy has a fixed range to read even if rows keep changing while it runs. The watermark moves forward only after the copy succeeds, so a failed run copies the same range again next time.

questions.stem: A 50,000-row reference table in an operational database has no change tracking and no reliable modified-date column, and rows are sometimes deleted. What load pattern fits best?

options.text: A watermark on the time the pipeline runs
A full load that replaces the destination table on each run
An incremental load with a watermark on the primary key
An append-only load that adds every source row on each run

questions.explanation: Without a change column an incremental load can't tell which rows changed, and no watermark ever sees a deleted row. At 50,000 rows a full replace is cheap and always matches the source. Appending every row on each run creates duplicates.

questions.stem: A pipeline copies changed rows by using two Lookup activities: one returns the saved watermark (OldWM) and one returns MAX(LastModifytime) from the source (NewWM). Which WHERE clause should the copy source query use so that no row is missed or copied twice across runs?

options.text: `WHERE LastModifytime >= OldWM AND LastModifytime < NewWM`
`WHERE LastModifytime > NewWM`
`WHERE LastModifytime >= OldWM`
`WHERE LastModifytime > OldWM AND LastModifytime <= NewWM`

questions.explanation: The old watermark was already loaded, so it is excluded with >, and the new watermark is included with <= because it is the value saved for the next run. The >= / < version reloads rows equal to OldWM and leaves rows at NewWM for later, and a query with no upper bound can pick up rows that change during the copy and then reload them.

questions.stem: A Copy job copies a SQL table into a lakehouse incrementally every hour. Last night one run failed partway through. What happens on the next run?

options.text: It skips the rows from the failed run and continues from the current time
It stops until someone resets the saved watermark by hand
It resumes from the end of the last successful run, so no data is lost
It starts again with a full copy of the whole table to rebuild the destination

questions.explanation: Copy job tracks the state of the last successful run and resumes from there. It doesn't fall back to a full copy, skip data, or need a manual reset.

questions.stem: You set up a Copy job from a SQL table that doesn't have CDC enabled but has a reliable ROWVERSION column. You only need inserts and updates. Which incremental method fits?

options.text: Incremental copy based on the last modified time of the source files
CDC-based incremental copy, after the job turns on CDC automatically
Full copy on every run with the overwrite update method
Watermark-based incremental copy on the ROWVERSION column

questions.explanation: Watermark-based incremental copy is the choice when CDC isn't available but a reliable incremental column such as ROWVERSION exists and only inserts and updates matter. CDC must already be enabled on the source, and a full copy rereads everything.

questions.stem: A Copy job must keep a lakehouse table in sync with a source database where rows are inserted, updated and deleted. CDC is enabled on the source. Which incremental method should you choose?

options.text: CDC-based incremental copy, merging into the destination
Full copy with the append update method
Watermark-based incremental copy on an integer key column
Watermark-based incremental copy on a datetime column

questions.explanation: Only CDC-based incremental copy replicates deletes; when merged into the destination, rows are inserted, updated or deleted. A watermark column can't show that a row was removed, and full copy with append duplicates rows.

questions.stem: A notebook reloads one month of sales into a Delta table. If the job is rerun, it must replace only that month's rows, with no duplicates and no change to other months. Which write fits?

options.text: `df.write.mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable("sales")`
`df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("sales")`
`df.write.mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", "sale_date >= '2026-10-01' AND sale_date < '2026-11-01'").saveAsTable("sales")`
`df.write.mode("ignore").saveAsTable("sales")`

questions.explanation: replaceWhere atomically overwrites only the rows that match the predicate, so a rerun replaces the month instead of adding it again. Append duplicates the month on a rerun, a plain overwrite replaces the whole table, and ignore writes nothing if the table exists.

questions.stem: Which two statements describe the default behavior of a Copy job? Each correct answer is a complete solution.

options.text: The Copy job doesn't delete any data in the destination
Destination tables are overwritten on every run unless you choose merge
Existing rows are merged on a key column unless you choose append
New data is appended to the destination, which keeps a full history
The first run of an incremental copy moves only rows changed since the job was created

questions.explanation: By default a Copy job appends and doesn't delete destination data; merge, overwrite and SCD type 2 are options you choose. The first incremental run copies everything, and later runs copy only changes.
